prototype.searchBound: The absence claims below are bounded by exactly this search, run at the pin in the sibling clone. Corpus: 5160 files after excluding node_modules and dist; 3775 of them TypeScript. (1) Case-insensitive ripgrep for permission|capabilit|consent|sandbox|egress|seccomp|apparmor|landlock|entitlement over the whole corpus, to find candidate surfaces. (2) Targeted reads of every hit in the capability/policy/bootstrap paths. (3) Case-insensitive ripgrep over TypeScript sources ONLY for the OS confinement primitives: sandbox-exec, sandbox_init, seccomp, landlock, apparmor, setrlimit, unshare, pledge(, chroot, CLONE_NEW, entitlement. RESULT: ZERO occurrences of any OS confinement primitive in TypeScript source. Every 'entitlement' hit is commercial licensing / cloud-plan entitlement (packages/output/src/sink/entitlement.ts and the host governance/audit/entitlements plane), which is unrelated to OS confinement; the remaining sandbox/seccomp/landlock hits are documentation and changelog prose, not code.
absenceClaimsWithinThatBound: NO OS-level or runtime-level confinement mechanism of any kind is invoked by the pinned prototype. The searched names are listed in searchBound and every one returned zero hits in TypeScript source. This is a statement about what the PROTOTYPE'S CODE DOES NOT CALL; it asserts nothing about whether any searched name exists, is available, or is usable on macOS or Linux, and none of them is nominated anywhere in this artifact as a V2 enforcement candidate.
NO network egress control exists at any layer other than the advisory in-process guard the prototype itself labels advisory.
NO filesystem confinement exists other than that same advisory guard's path checks, which the module states cannot be made sound in-process.

NO revocation, grant generation, expiry, or durable permission journal exists. The prototype's decision is computed at admission and carried in memory for the process's life; there is no linearization point, no revocation record, and nothing to order.
NO irreversible-effect boundary, completed-before-revocation disclosure, or indeterminate-outcome handling exists, because there is no revocation to be racing.

coverageObligation.source: docs/v2/architecture/03-configuration-and-security.md, measured at digest: 'Every platform needs a truth table for filesystem, network, subprocess, state, secret-handle, artifact, and other effects.'
coverageObligation.rule: Every member of that seven-member enumeration appears below either as a minted token, an explicitly RESERVED extension point with its minting owner, or a deliberate non-token with its reason. None is silently dropped, and none is silently invented past.

mapping.filesystem: MINTED: PT-FS-READ-PROJECT, PT-FS-READ-COMPONENT, PT-FS-WRITE-HOST-STATE. RESERVED: fs.write.project (no slice-1 command mutates project files).
mapping.network: MINTED: PT-NET-EGRESS, deny-by-default, reachable in slice 1 only through DR-114 consent. RESERVED: inbound/listening.
mapping.subprocess: MINTED: PT-PROC-EXEC-DECLARED, bounded to programs declared in the admitted immutable tree. RESERVED: argument-vector scoping.
mapping.state: MINTED: PT-FS-WRITE-HOST-STATE for direct writes and PT-HOST-EFFECT-BROKERED for the brokered state route. Which classes exist is DR-124's (ID-DEP-P5); authoritative evidence is out of slice 1 wholly per D-002.
mapping.secret-handle: RESERVED, not minted -- DR-108 deferred by D-002 ('no credential-requiring features in slice 1').
mapping.artifact: RESERVED, not minted -- the slice-1 artifact surface would be authoritative evidence custody, which D-002 excludes wholly.
mapping.other effects: MINTED: PT-ENV-READ, PT-HOST-EFFECT-BROKERED. DELIBERATE NON-TOKENS with reasons: clock, entropy, host output, host-initiated writes to a user-named output path. CLOSURE RULE: anything not enumerated is denied by absence and decides PR-3 if declared.

permissionVocabulary.closure: CLOSED at seven tokens. The set is closed in the strong sense: a token outside it is not 'unrecognized and ignored', it is a refusal (PR-3). Closure is what makes the manifest candidate's UNKNOWN_PERMISSION_TOKEN decidable, and it is what enforces file 03's law that a manifest, repository, or publisher cannot grant authority to itself -- an open vocabulary would let a manifest name its own authority into existence.
permissionVocabulary.whyThisGranularity: The prototype's four coarse classes (filesystem/network/env/subprocess) were measured and are NARROWED AND SPLIT rather than carried. Filesystem splits three ways because project reads, component-closure reads, and host-state writes have different justifications, different reversibility, and different consequences when denied -- collapsing them would make a project-read denial silently disable a component's own bundled runtime. Environment stays whole because its enforcement mechanism operates on the whole environment block at once. The brokered route is added because file 02's fifth permitted function has no counterpart in the prototype's set.

tokens.meaning: Read bytes at paths resolved inside the project root the operation is bound to, as the host resolved that root; symlink targets are resolved before the containment test, so a link inside the root that resolves outside is outside.
tokens.sliceJustification: D-002's slice ships `analyze` over a project tree; a TypeScript analyzer that cannot read project sources performs no analysis. This is the 'local read' half of D-002's own DR-105 scoping ('scoped to the permissions the slice actually exercises: local read/write + consented doctor probes').
tokens.scopeParameter: Optional path-prefix list relative to the project root; absent means the whole resolved root. The scope is data on the grant, not a claim that the bound is imposed on the component.
tokens.reversibility: REVERSIBLE-BY-CLASS (a read commits no external state). Reads still journal acceptance, because a read of a denied path is the refusal this token exists to record.

tokens.meaning: Read bytes inside the component's own immutable installed tree, as admitted.
tokens.sliceJustification: A component reads its own bundled runtime/parser closure; DR-119 (D-008, accepted universally) requires that closure to ship with the component, so reading it is structural to every supported role rather than optional. Splitting it from PT-FS-READ-PROJECT keeps a project-read denial from silently disabling a component's own closure.
tokens.scopeParameter: None. The scope is exactly the admitted immutable tree; there is no sub-path form, because a component that needs less than its own tree gains nothing recordable by saying so.

tokens.meaning: Create, modify, or remove bytes inside the host-owned state namespace allocated to this component for its declared state class.
tokens.sliceJustification: D-002's slice admits exactly two state classes -- rebuildable cache/index and operational metadata (DR-124) -- and both need a writer. The token is the 'local write' half of D-002's DR-105 scoping. It never reaches authoritative evidence, which D-002 excludes from slice 1 wholly.
tokens.scopeParameter: The declared state class plus the host-allocated namespace path for this component. Which classes exist and who may write them is DR-124's, not this artifact's (ID-DEP-P5).
tokens.reversibility: CONDITIONALLY-REVERSIBLE: reversible only for a write the host staged (temporary write plus rename, with the prior bytes retained until cleanup closes). A direct in-place write by the component is IRREVERSIBLE to the host, because the host never held the prior bytes.

tokens.meaning: Execute a program that the admitted manifest declared, from inside the component's own admitted immutable tree, as a child process.
tokens.sliceJustification: DR-119's self-contained-closure rule (D-008) puts a role's parser/compiler/language-server-class dependencies inside the component; running them is process execution. Restricting the token's meaning to programs declared in the admitted tree is what keeps it from becoming a general execute-anything grant, which freeze law 11 (file 03, repository-code execution default) forbids by default.
tokens.scopeParameter: The declared program identifiers. Argument vectors are NOT scoped by this token; argument-level policy is not designed here and is a RESERVED extension point.
tokens.reversibility: IRREVERSIBLE by default. A spawned process may have done anything before the host observes its exit; the host holds no inverse.

tokens.meaning: Initiate an outbound network connection or request.
tokens.sliceJustification: D-002's architecture preview is offline and file 04 makes doctor no-network by default. Adopted D-032 places host-under-instruction outside this vocabulary: doctor's own socket is host CA-4, not this token. This token covers COMPONENT-ORIGINATED egress only: an admitted component child produced by a host CA-1 SPAWN decision, or any other admitted component. It does not cover CA-2 customer-tool later effects; those are neither admitted-component PT-NET-EGRESS nor host CA-4 (named at recorded actor-join v6 / D-127 and recorded host-effect v8/v25). The v2/v6 parenthetical 'a process doctor spawned under CA-1/CA-2' is superseded. Host consent cannot substitute. It is enumerated rather than omitted because absence-denies needs a name to deny on the component tail. If the preview never admits a networked component, the token remains DENIED by default and has no granted preview exerciser.
tokens.scopeParameter: Endpoint set as named by the consent record. This artifact does not design the endpoint grammar; DR-114 owns the consent contract (ID-DEP-P3).
tokens.reversibility: IRREVERSIBLE, always and by class. Once bytes leave the host, no host-side record can retract them. This is stated as a class rule so that no future effect-class declaration can mark an egress reversible.

tokens.meaning: Read the value of a named environment variable that the host places in the component process's own environment block.
tokens.sliceJustification: The pinned prototype's measured requirement shape carries `env` with a per-variable `scope` (resource-requirement.ts, measured at digest), and the prototype's worker environment is CONSTRUCTED from an allowlist rather than inherited (env.ts / build-external-worker-child-env.ts, measured). This is the one token in the slice whose grant/denial has a nameable POSIX mechanism, which is why it is a token in its own right and not folded into a generic configuration surface.
tokens.scopeParameter: The exact variable names. A prefix or pattern form is deliberately NOT defined: a pattern would make the granted set depend on the host's ambient environment at spawn time, which is not a declared input.
tokens.reversibility: REVERSIBLE-BY-CLASS as an act (a read commits nothing), IRREVERSIBLE in consequence (a value the component has read cannot be un-read). The vocabulary keeps these apart deliberately -- see linearization.effectCommitDefinitions.

tokens.meaning: Open a brokered-effect request at all: the right to send `effectRequest` on the control channel and have the host consider it. It is NOT itself an effect class. Every individual request still names one of the other tokens above as the effect it asks the host to perform on the component's behalf.
tokens.sliceJustification: File 02's fifth permitted control-plane function is 'broker separately authorized host effects'; the candidate control-protocol contract (measured at digest) carries it as `effectRequest`/`effectResult` and refuses an unauthorized one at RF-6. Without a token gating the route itself, a component with every effect token denied could still generate unbounded refused traffic, and the manifest would have no way to declare that it uses the broker at all.
tokens.scopeParameter: The set of effect tokens the component may name in a request, which must be a subset of its granted tokens. Deny wins: a token denied directly is denied through the broker.
tokens.reversibility: Inherits the reversibility of the effect token the request names. The route itself commits nothing.

deliberateNonTokens.ruling: NOT a permission token in this vocabulary.
deliberateNonTokens.why: Two independent reasons, both measured. (1) Permissioning it would be unenforceable disclosure at best on both platforms: a same-user process reads the clock with no host mediation and no call the host can interpose. (2) Its actual hazard is not authority but determinism -- a component that reads the clock has taken an undeclared Plan input, which file 04 makes a DR-124/DR-G19 negative test ('Cross-class writes, cache-to-authority promotion, undeclared Plan inputs, and component evidence commits are negative tests under DR-124 and DR-G19'). Routing it here would move a determinism obligation onto a surface that cannot carry it.
deliberateNonTokens.whereItBelongs: DR-124/DR-G19 undeclared-Plan-input negative tests, and DR-G09's own standing prohibition that wall-clock ordering is forbidden (register, DR-G09 waiver-rule cell: 'wall-clock/component ordering is forbidden'), which this artifact's linearization obeys structurally.

deliberateNonTokens.ruling: NOT a permission token in this vocabulary.
deliberateNonTokens.why: Same two reasons as clock, and the same owner. Unmediatable for a same-user process, and semantically a determinism concern rather than an authority concern.

File 02 already forbids components from rendering product UI, choosing verdicts/exits, or writing unstructured host logs, and the candidate control-protocol contract makes stdout/stderr structurally the provider data plane and bounded diagnostics respectively. A permission token would imply the alternative is grantable; it is not.

deliberateNonTokens.candidate: host-initiated writes to a user-named output path (e.g. `analyze --output report.sarif`)
deliberateNonTokens.ruling: NOT a component permission, and not in the truth table.
deliberateNonTokens.why: The actor is the host, under the invoking user's direct instruction on the command line. Treating it as a permission would model the user as needing authorization against themselves, which file 03's law -- that authority is not self-granted -- is not about.
deliberateNonTokens.whereItBelongs: DR-123's CLI baseline and DR-G17's serialization-failure behavior.

reservedExtensionPoints.why: No command in D-002's slice mutates project files: `analyze` is read-only over the project and doctor 'defaults to read-only, no component code, no network, and no mutation' (file 04). Minting a token no slice-1 surface exercises would put an unexercised grant path in the vocabulary, and its truth-table row would be a claim about a mechanism nothing runs.
reservedExtensionPoints.whoMints: The first slice decision that admits a project-mutating command, with its own scope disposition per D-002's discipline that every scoped inclusion is recorded with its own artifact and commit.

columnSemantics.framing: File 03 splits per-operation permission resolution into two records, and this table keeps them apart in the same way: AUTHORIZATION (requested, then granted or denied) and EXECUTION (enforced, disclosed-trusted-code, or refused). The five columns the DR-105 row names are laid over that split.
columnSemantics.REQUESTED: An AUTHORIZATION record. A declaration in the admitted manifest. Confers nothing.
columnSemantics.GRANTED: An AUTHORIZATION record. Resolution to granted, durably ordered. Confers PERMISSION, not CAPABILITY. On a DISCLOSURE-ONLY row it changes nothing about what the component can do.
columnSemantics.DENIED: An AUTHORIZATION record. Resolution to denied, or absence, or a matching deny rule. On a DISCLOSURE-ONLY row it means the host will not act on the brokered route -- not that the effect did not occur.
columnSemantics.ENFORCED: An EXECUTION fact, and the load-bearing column. Its value is one of the four in enforcementStateVocabulary, split by execution mode, with a named mechanism required for every enforced value and a stated scope of claim for every value.
columnSemantics.DISCLOSED: An OBLIGATION on the host's output and audit, derived from the ENFORCED value. Silence is not disclosure; an absent ENFORCED field is not equivalent to a DISCLOSURE-ONLY one.
columnSemantics.theRuleThisTableExistsToHold: REQUESTED and GRANTED must never read as ENFORCED, in this table, in any output derived from it, or in any summary of it. A row whose ENFORCED value is DISCLOSURE-ONLY describes a component that is trusted code in the TCB for that effect class, and the DISCLOSED column obliges the host to say so affirmatively.

enforcementStateVocabulary.ENFORCED-BY-CONSTRUCTION: The capability is never conferred on the component, so the denied effect has no path that the host would have to interpose on. A named mechanism is required for this value and is recorded in the cell.
enforcementStateVocabulary.ENFORCED-AT-HOST-BROKER: The host is the actor for the brokered route: it decides, and its refusal is total FOR THAT ROUTE. This value carries a mandatory paired disclosure, because file 03 states that host brokers used voluntarily by an unconstrained same-user process do not create confinement.
enforcementStateVocabulary.DISCLOSURE-ONLY: No mechanism prevents the effect. The grant record is a record of what was asked and answered, and the component is disclosed trusted code in the TCB per file 02: 'an unconstrained same-user component remains trusted code in the TCB unless effective confinement is enforced and measured.' A DISCLOSURE-ONLY cell must never be reported, rendered, or summarized as enforcement.
enforcementStateVocabulary.OPEN: This artifact has not determined the value and names who must. Reserved for genuine non-determination; it is not a placeholder for a value the authoring session simply preferred not to state.

theOrder.carrier: ONE durable, append-only grant journal per (project, grant generation), with exactly one writer: the host, holding the project/operation lock. There is no second ordering authority anywhere in this design.
theOrder.sequence: Every record carries a strictly increasing unsigned integer sequence number assigned by the single writer. The next sequence number is derived from the journal itself -- last durably committed sequence plus one -- so the counter cannot diverge from the bytes that define it, and a crash cannot resurrect a number that was never durable.
theOrder.durabilityRule: A record is ORDERED when and only when its bytes are durable. 'Durably ordered before' means: its sequence number is lower AND it is present after crash recovery replays the journal. A sequence number assigned in memory but not yet durable orders NOTHING and gates NOTHING; every gate in the race semantics below is stated against the durable record, never against the in-memory assignment.
theOrder.monotonicityAcrossCrash: Recovery replays the journal from its start (or from the last durable checkpoint record, which is itself a journal record) and resumes at last-durable-plus-one. Sequence numbers are never reused, never reordered, and never renumbered by migration; a migration that rewrote them would be rewriting history, which file 04's state-class rule forbids for the class this journal would belong to.
theOrder.whatIsForbiddenAsAnOrDER: Wall-clock time, monotonic-clock readings, message arrival order, process scheduling order, component-supplied ordinals, and any component-influenced value. This obeys DR-G09's own waiver rule as written in the register: 'wall-clock/component ordering is forbidden'. Timestamps MAY be recorded as DATA on a record for operator legibility; a timestamp is never read to decide precedence, and a fixture class (FX-7) exists to prove the ordering is invariant to clock manipulation.
theOrder.whyOneJournalAndNotPerGrant: File 03 requires 'one durable, monotonic revocation linearization point per grant generation'. A per-generation journal gives that point a byte address rather than a concept: the revocation record's own sequence number IS the linearization point. Comparing two grants in different generations is not defined and is not needed -- no rule in this contract compares across generations.

transitions.guarantees: The host has resolved a brokered request against the grant and durably recorded that it will consider performing the effect. RA guarantees NO effect has been initiated. Nothing external has happened at RA and nothing external may happen until a commit-intent record is durable.
transitions.afterCrash: An RA with no successor record means the request was accepted and never committed. Recovery treats it as CANCELED-BY-RECOVERY. This is safe without inspecting the world, because no effect can precede its own commit-intent record.

transitions.guarantees: The host is about to perform an effect for which it holds an inverse it can journal and re-run. Written and made durable BEFORE the effect is initiated.
transitions.afterCrash: An RCI with no outcome record means the effect may or may not have landed. Because the class declared an inverse, recovery RUNS the inverse (which must be idempotent) and records CLEANUP. No indeterminacy is disclosed, because the host can restore the prior state either way.

transitions.guarantees: The reversible effect completed or failed, recorded exactly. Until cleanup closes, the inverse remains available.

THIS RECORD IS THE EFFECT-COMMIT POINT. It is written and made durable BEFORE the host initiates the external irreversible effect, and its sequence number is what every revocation comparison in this contract is stated against. File 03's phrase 'an irreversible external effect whose host-owned effect-commit was durably ordered before revocation' is given its byte address here and nowhere else.
transitions.afterCrash: An ICI with no outcome record is the hardest state in this design and gets the honest answer rather than a convenient one -- see irreversibleBoundary.indeterminateOutcome.

transitions.guarantees: Records COMPLETED, FAILED, or INDETERMINATE. INDETERMINATE is a first-class value of this record, not an error path.
transitions.afterCrash: Terminal. The recorded value stands; recovery never re-derives or upgrades it.

transitions.guarantees: The revocation linearization point for this grant generation. Its sequence number r is the single number that every race in this contract resolves against. Once REV is durable: no record of type RA, RCI, or ICI may be written for this generation at any sequence greater than r. Not 'should not' -- the single writer refuses to write one, and a written one is a defect that fixture class FX-5 exists to detect.
transitions.afterCrash: Recovery reads REV and enters the revoked state before processing anything else at a higher sequence.

transitions.guarantees: Bounded cancellation and cleanup for the generation have finished: every reversible effect with an available inverse has had it run, every handle and grant is closed, and the residual set is fixed. 'Bounded' means the cleanup has a declared bound and reaching that bound without closure is itself journaled as a residual, not retried without limit.
transitions.afterCrash: Cleanup re-runs from the journal; every inverse is required to be idempotent by its class declaration, so re-running is safe by construction rather than by care.

transitions.guarantees: The audit binding is complete for the generation. File 03's binding list, carried whole: acceptance, effect-commit, revocation, cleanup, and residual outcome, each bound to the grant generation, the process descendant, the Run/operation, and the broker request IDs. The identities of Run/operation are NOT minted here and ride DR-006's parked recipes (ID-DEP-P12).
transitions.afterCrash: An unsealed generation is disclosed as unsealed. Recovery does not seal it retroactively.

effectCommitDefinitions.rule: Reversibility is a declared property of an EFFECT CLASS, never inferred per request and never asserted by a component.
effectCommitDefinitions.default: IRREVERSIBLE. An effect class is irreversible unless it declares a host-owned, journaled, idempotent inverse WHOSE OWN FAILURE IS DETECTABLE BY THE HOST. Defaulting to irreversible is the fail-closed direction: mislabeling an irreversible effect as reversible would let revocation claim an undo that never happened, which is the exact dishonesty file 03's completed-before-revocation clause exists to prevent.

byToken.PT-NET-EGRESS: IRREVERSIBLE by class rule, not by declaration. No future effect-class declaration may mark an egress reversible; bytes that left the host are not retractable by any host-side record.
byToken.PT-PROC-EXEC-DECLARED: IRREVERSIBLE. The host holds no inverse for whatever a spawned process did before it was reaped.
byToken.PT-FS-WRITE-HOST-STATE: CONDITIONALLY REVERSIBLE, and only for a HOST-STAGED write in which the host retained the prior bytes until CLN. A direct component write is irreversible to the host, which never held the prior bytes -- and on a DISCLOSURE-ONLY row the component's direct write is precisely what the host cannot prevent, so this condition is doing real work rather than decorating.
byToken.PT-FS-READ-PROJECT / PT-FS-READ-COMPONEN: The ACT commits no external state. The CONSEQUENCE is irreversible: a value read cannot be un-read. These are kept apart deliberately: reads take the reversible path for cleanup purposes, and revocation after a read is never described as having withdrawn the information.

irreversibleBoundary.theRule: Let r be the sequence number of REV and n the sequence number of the effect's ICI. Exactly two cases exist and there is no third: (a) n < r -- the effect-commit was durably ordered before revocation; (b) r < n -- it was not. n = r is impossible: sequence numbers are unique per journal and there is one writer.
irreversibleBoundary.caseBefore: n < r. BEFORE-REVOCATION is the ORDERING property (file 03's completed-before-revocation clause names the ordering, not the ICO value). Disclosure is derived from the ICO value carried alongside that property: ICO=COMPLETED discloses COMPLETED-BEFORE-REVOCATION and is not falsely reported undone; ICO=FAILED discloses FAILED-BEFORE-REVOCATION (the commit was ordered before revocation, the effect did not land, revocation did not reach it, and no undo is claimed); ICO=INDETERMINATE discloses INDETERMINATE-BEFORE-REVOCATION. Revocation does not reach any of the three. COMPLETED-BEFORE-REVOCATION is not an outcome competing with FAILED or INDETERMINATE.
irreversibleBoundary.caseAfter: r < n is unreachable by construction: after REV is durable the single writer refuses to write an ICI for this generation, so an irreversible effect not yet committed at the revocation point is FORBIDDEN and is never initiated. File 03: 'An irreversible effect not yet committed at the point is forbidden.'

whatRevocationMeansAfterAnIrreversibleCo.statement: Revocation after an irreversible effect has committed means exactly these four things and nothing else.
itMeans: 1. FUTURE REQUESTS ARE BARRED. No RA is written for this generation at any sequence above r; a brokered request arriving afterwards is refused (PR-5).
2. LATER USE BY THE COMPONENT AND EVERY DESCENDANT IS INVALIDATED, on the brokered route -- file 03's clause, with its honest bound stated at raceSemantics R-8 rather than left implied.
3. BOUNDED CANCELLATION AND CLEANUP RUN for everything still reversible, terminating at CLN.

4. DISCLOSURE IS OWED. The before-revocation effect appears in the audit and in the operator-facing residual outcome, disclosed as COMPLETED-BEFORE-REVOCATION, FAILED-BEFORE-REVOCATION, or INDETERMINATE-BEFORE-REVOCATION according to the ICO value, never softened to a single 'completed' wording over a FAILED or INDETERMINATE ICO. Disclosure is an obligation created BY the revocation, not a side effect of it.
itDoesNotMean: It does not mean undone, reversed, rolled back, compensated, neutralized, contained, or mitigated. The host must not emit any string implying any of those about a completed-before-revocation effect; fixture class FX-6 is a wording-level golden over exactly this, because this is a place where honest mechanics have historically been narrated away at the output layer.

It does not create a compensating action. If a future surface adds compensation, a compensating action is a NEW effect: it needs its own authorization, its own ICI/ICO records at its own sequence numbers, and its own disclosure. It is never folded into the revocation record and never presented as the revocation having worked.
It does not change the residual outcome. The residual is what it was at r.

indeterminateOutcome.state: An ICI is durable and no ICO follows -- the host died between committing its intent and recording what happened.
indeterminateOutcome.ruling: Recovery records ICO = INDETERMINATE and discloses it. It does NOT guess, does NOT retry, does NOT assume failure, and does NOT assume success.
indeterminateOutcome.why: The host cannot observe the external world's state; it can only observe its own records. Any of the three convenient answers would be a claim the host has no basis for, and 'assume failed then retry' is the most dangerous of them -- it converts an unknown single effect into a known double effect.
indeterminateOutcome.consequence: The grant generation is treated as revoked at recovery (fail-closed), the INDETERMINATE residual is carried into AUD, and the operator is told which effect is in an unknown state and why the host cannot say more. An INDETERMINATE that is later resolved by external means is a new record, never an edit.

irreversibleBoundary.orderingIsOverRecordsNotWorldEvents: Stated plainly because it bounds every claim above: this order is a total order over the HOST'S OWN DURABLE RECORDS. It is not a total order over events in the external world, and the host does not and cannot observe the instant at which an external effect actually took place. Every 'before'/'after' in this contract means 'before/after in the journal'. A reader who needs to know what the world did at wall-clock time t does not get it from this design, and no fixture class here supplies it.

raceSemantics.discipline: Each race states the DETERMINISTIC OUTCOME, not a preference and not a 'should'. Every outcome below is decided by comparing sequence numbers in one journal written by one writer; no rule consults a clock, an arrival order, a timeout, or a component-supplied value.

races.race: An ALREADY-ACCEPTED request (RA durable at sequence a) when revocation lands at r > a, with no commit-intent yet written.
races.outcome: The request is CANCELED. No effect is initiated. The outcome recorded against the request is refusal family PR-5 (grant-revoked), and cleanup for it is a no-op that still closes at CLN.
races.whyDeterministic: The single writer refuses to write RCI or ICI above r. Acceptance is not permission to commit; only a durable commit-intent is, and that record cannot exist.

races.race: An IN-FLIGHT request at revocation time: RA is durable, the host is mid-way through preparing the effect, revocation arrives.
races.outcome: The commit-intent write is the ONLY gate, and it either became durable at a sequence below r or it did not. If it did not, it never will, the effect is never initiated, and the request refuses PR-5. There is no window in which an effect is initiated without a durable intent record ordered below r.
races.whyDeterministic: Initiation strictly follows durable intent, by L-2/L-4. 'In flight' is therefore not a third state between accepted and committed; it is a state in which the deciding record has not yet been written, and the single writer decides it with a comparison of integers -- no timer, no clock, no message-arrival comparison.

races.outcome: Resolved wholly by n versus r per irreversibleBoundary.theRule. n < r: before-revocation ordering, disclosed per ICO (COMPLETED-BEFORE-REVOCATION / FAILED-BEFORE-REVOCATION / INDETERMINATE-BEFORE-REVOCATION), not undone. r < n: unreachable -- the ICI is never written, the effect is never initiated.
races.whyDeterministic: Two integers from one writer in one journal. The external world's timing is not consulted and cannot change the answer -- which is exactly why the claim is bounded to the records (irreversibleBoundary.orderingIsOverRecordsNotWorldEvents).

races.race: CONCURRENT requests for the SAME token, from the same component or from a component and its descendant.
races.outcome: Serialized by the single writer into distinct sequence numbers. Both are accepted -- a token grant is NOT exclusive by default -- unless the effect class declares exclusivity, in which case the LOWER sequence number wins and the higher refuses PR-9 (exclusivity-conflict). The loser is never queued, retried, or promoted when the winner finishes.
races.whyDeterministic: The winner is decided by sequence number, not by arrival, not by which thread got the lock first as observed by a clock, and not by component-supplied priority.

races.race: REVOCATION DURING CLEANUP: a second REV arrives for a generation already revoked and mid-cleanup.
races.outcome: Recorded as a duplicate revocation record with its own sequence number and NO state change. Cleanup is not restarted, not extended, not aborted, and its bound is not reset. CLN still closes exactly once.
races.whyDeterministic: Revocation is idempotent at the state level and non-idempotent at the record level -- every revocation attempt is journaled, exactly one is the linearization point (the first, at r), and later ones are audit facts.

races.outcome: Recovery re-runs cleanup from the journal. Every inverse is idempotent by its effect class's own declaration, so re-running is safe by construction. Cleanup's bound is measured from the recovery, and exhausting it journals a residual rather than looping.
races.whyDeterministic: Idempotence is a precondition of an effect class being called reversible at all, per effectCommitDefinitions.default -- so this case needs no special reasoning, which is the point of putting the requirement in the definition.

races.race: REVOCATION BEFORE ACCEPTANCE: a brokered request whose acceptance would land above r.
races.outcome: DENIED. File 03, carried whole: 'A broker request whose acceptance is not durably ordered before that point is denied.' Refusal family PR-5.
races.whyDeterministic: The single writer will not write an RA above r for a revoked generation.

races.race: A DESCENDANT PROCESS using the grant after revocation.
races.outcome: Every brokered request on any channel bound to the revoked generation is refused, PR-5, whether it came from the component or any descendant. THE HONEST BOUND, which is the whole content of this row: that is enforced for the BROKERED ROUTE ONLY. A descendant holding ambient authority is unaffected by revocation, the host neither observes nor records what it does, and on every DISCLOSURE-ONLY cell in the truth table that is the ordinary case rather than the exotic one. Fixture class FX-8 asserts BOTH halves -- the brokered refusal AND the ambient success -- so that the evidence cannot be read as confinement.
races.whyDeterministic: For the brokered half: the generation is revoked and the writer refuses. For the ambient half: there is nothing to be deterministic about, which is the disclosure.

races.race: A request naming a token that is granted, at a SCOPE wider than the grant, racing a scope narrowing.
races.outcome: The grant's scope at the request's own accepted sequence number is the one that applies; a narrowing is itself a journaled record with its own sequence number, and a request accepted above it is evaluated against the narrowed scope. Over-scope refuses PR-4.
races.whyDeterministic: Scope changes are records in the same single order as everything else. There is no separate configuration-reload path that could change a grant's scope without a sequence number.

races.race: An EXPIRY falling between acceptance and commit-intent.
races.outcome: Expiry is materialized as a journaled record at the sequence where the host observes it, and it behaves exactly as REV from that point (bar future requests, cancel and clean up what is reversible, disclose what completed). It is NOT evaluated by comparing a wall-clock expiry timestamp against a wall-clock now at commit time; doing so would make the clock the order, which DR-G09 forbids.
races.whyDeterministic: The expiry RECORD, not the expiry TIME, is what other records are ordered against.

refusalFamilies.discipline: STRUCTURE ONLY. These are permission-decision classes. They are NOT exit codes, NOT D9 codes, NOT fates, and this artifact assigns no VALUE to any of them -- DR-007's successor chain owns that mapping and is HARD-BLOCKED (identityDependencies ID-DEP-P1). The naming discipline is copied from the candidate control-protocol contract's own refusal-family rule rather than invented alongside it.
refusalFamilies.relationToTheControlPlane: These families REFINE the candidate control-protocol contract's RF-6 (unauthorized-host-effect); they do not parallel it. RF-6 is the WIRE class -- what the control channel reports when a brokered request is not authorized. PR-1..PR-9 are the DECISION classes the host reached before that report was written. One RF-6 on the wire carries exactly one PR-n as its decision. No new wire family is proposed by this artifact, and no PR-n is a control-plane message; a permission decision that never reaches a component (a denial at admission, PR-1) has a PR class and no RF at all.

families.name: token-not-declared
families.covers: The effect's token is absent from the admitted manifest's permissions block. Absence denies (file 03). Reached at admission or at request evaluation; when reached at admission there is no wire refusal, because there is no request.

families.name: token-denied
families.covers: The token was declared and the host resolved it to denied. Deny wins; a manifest, repository, or publisher cannot grant authority to itself (file 03).

families.name: token-outside-vocabulary
families.covers: The declared token is not a member of this contract's closed set and is not a minted extension point. This is the decision class that makes the candidate manifest schema's UNKNOWN_PERMISSION_TOKEN subcode decidable -- see closesFromThisSide.

families.name: scope-exceeded
families.covers: The token is granted but the request falls outside the granted scope (a path outside the granted prefix, a variable name not granted, an endpoint outside the consent record, a program not declared).

families.name: grant-revoked-or-expired
families.covers: The request's acceptance would order at or above the revocation/expiry record for this grant generation. Covers R-1, R-2, R-7, R-8's brokered half, and R-10.

families.name: required-confinement-unenforceable
families.covers: An effect whose policy REQUIRES confinement is requested on a platform and mode where confinement is not enforced. File 03: 'Required confinement refuses when unenforceable.' NOTE, reported not resolved: no measured source enumerates WHICH effects require confinement -- see tensionsObserved T-1 -- so this family's TRIGGER SET is empty in this artifact and the family exists so that the eventual enumeration has a place to land, not so that it can be quietly skipped.

families.name: consent-required-and-unavailable
families.covers: Trusted-code fallback or a consented probe/egress is needed and no consent exists. File 03, carried whole: consent must be 'bound to exact component bytes, operation, scope, and platform', and 'CI never prompts and needs pre-existing policy'. In a non-interactive context this family is reached WITHOUT attempting a prompt; attempting one is itself the defect FX-9 detects.

families.name: irreversible-effect-forbidden-at-this-point
families.covers: An irreversible effect whose commit-intent would order above the revocation point. Distinguished from PR-5 deliberately: PR-5 is about the grant, PR-8 is about the effect's own irreversibility, and collapsing them would lose the distinction that makes the completed-before-revocation disclosure legible.

families.name: exclusivity-conflict
families.covers: An effect class declaring exclusivity already has a lower-sequence holder (R-4).

notRefusals: INDETERMINATE is an OUTCOME, not a refusal. A refusal means the host did not perform the effect; INDETERMINATE means the host does not know. Modeling it as a refusal would let a summary count it among the effects that did not happen.
COMPLETED-BEFORE-REVOCATION is an OUTCOME, not a refusal, for the same reason and with more force.

acceptanceEvidenceFixtureClasses.discipline: SPECIFICATIONS OF EXACT-BYTE INTENT, not implementations. No fixture exists; no harness runs; nothing here is executed evidence. Each class carries a MANDATORY `proves` field with exactly one of two values, because the DR-105 row asks for 'enforcement evidence' and a test that only shows a request was recorded is evidence of DISCLOSURE. Mislabeling the second as the first is the single most likely way this row could be closed dishonestly, so the labeling is structural rather than editorial.

provesVocabulary.ENFORCEMENT: The fixture's assertion fails if the effect is POSSIBLE. It tests a mechanism.
provesVocabulary.DISCLOSURE: The fixture's assertion fails only if the RECORD is wrong. It tests bookkeeping. A DISCLOSURE-class fixture can pass in full while the component performs every denied effect at will.

classes.name: vocabulary closure
classes.intent: A manifest declaring a token outside the closed set is refused at admission with decision class PR-3, and a manifest declaring every member of the closed set is admitted. Exact bytes: the admitted/refused decision record for each of the seven tokens plus a corpus of non-members (near-misses, case variants, whitespace variants, and the pinned prototype's four coarse class strings `filesystem`/`network`/`env`/`subprocess`, which are NOT V2 tokens and must refuse).

classes.name: absence-denies, brokered route
classes.intent: For each token, a component whose manifest omits it issues a brokered request for it; assert the request is refused PR-1 and that no host effect record was written. Exact bytes: the refusal record and the journal segment showing no RCI/ICI.

classes.name: the negative-space fixture -- ambient path succeeds
classes.proves: DISCLOSURE (and it proves the ABSENCE of enforcement, deliberately)
classes.intent: The same component, with the same token denied, performs the same effect DIRECTLY via ambient authority, and the fixture ASSERTS THAT IT SUCCEEDS. A read outside the granted prefix reads; a denied egress connects; a denied exec execs. Exact bytes: the effect's own observable result, plus the host's journal showing it recorded nothing.
